title: Expansion furnishing fabric
lede: Barbara Brown’s screen-printed furnishing fabric for Heal’s: black bands that narrow, bend, and converge so that the cloth seems to bulge.
summary: Black undulating stripes on white that pinch together and swell, in a large repeat. Barbara Brown for Heal’s, 1966.

creator.name: Barbara Brown (designer); Heal’s Wholesale & Export Ltd (manufacturer)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.269-1967 (1165 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A clear op furnishing print: black and white stripes that change width by steps to suggest swelling and depth.

context: The V&A catalogues the fabric with the style “Op art” and describes screen-printed cotton satin “with wide stripes in optical black-and-white undulating stripes giving the illusion of three-dimensionality”, 108 × 48 in. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O224418/).

The V&A’s Heal’s records say that 1960s Heal’s furnishing textiles moved from sober geometry “through Pop and Op Art-inspired motifs” to flower-power florals, under design consultant Tom Worthington. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O46802/).
observed: Pure black on white. Three identical horizontal repeats fill the length.
In each repeat, vertical black bands pinch to hair-thin lines at the centre and widen into heavy wave shapes toward the edges.
At the top and bottom of each repeat, the bands fan out into points, so each repeat reads as a swelling drum or waist.
Selvedge printing along both edges gives the designer, the title, and the maker.
interpretation: Expansion uses the op device of progression: stripe width alone creates a curved surface on flat cloth.
It shows the style at furnishing scale, where one repeat is about the height of a person.
borrow: Make a band narrow toward a centre line and widen toward the edges to suggest a bulge.
Repeat one large, symmetric unit vertically so that the whole panel reads as one field.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Barbara Brown’s design is in copyright, and the V&A image is not openly licensed.
